title: Looking under the lamp
hookLine: he lost his key inside the house but searches the street, because the light is better there

lines: A NEW KIND OF TEACHER: A FOOL.
THE STORIES BELONG TO THE TELLERS.
cards: This week's teacher isn't an emperor or a philosopher. He's a fool. Or someone who looks like one.
His name is Nasruddin. In Turkey he's Nasreddin Hodja; in Iran and Central Asia, Mulla Nasruddin.
People have told short, funny stories about him for a long time, in many lands: at weddings, in coffee shops, to children at bedtime. Nobody knows for sure whether he was one real man.
The stories belong to the people who tell them. Here's one.

teach.h: ON HIS KNEES UNDER A LAMP.
teach.b: It's night. A neighbor finds Nasruddin on his hands and knees in the street, under a lamp. What have you lost, Mulla?
My key, he says. So the neighbor gets down and helps. They search a long time: every stone, every crack.
Nothing. Finally the neighbor asks: where exactly did you lose it?

teach.h: I LOST IT INSIDE THE HOUSE.
teach.b: Oh, says Nasruddin, inside the house. Then why on earth are we looking out here?
Because there's more light here. It's a joke, and you're allowed to laugh.
That's how these stories work: first you laugh at the fool, and a few seconds later it's easy to notice he might be you.
Looking where it's easy to look, not where things are, is a very human habit. Scientists even have a name for it now: the streetlight effect, studying what's easy to measure instead of what matters.
People do it with bigger things than keys. Looking for peace in the next purchase, when the restlessness is somewhere inside.
Looking for the fix to a relationship in a new city, when the trouble came along in the suitcase.
Some Sufi teachers have told this tale as a picture of the soul, searching the bright outside world for something lost within. But the tale itself doesn't explain. Nasruddin stories rarely do.
They just leave you standing in the street with the fool, both of you holding a very good lamp, and both of you knowing, now, where the key really is.

how: Nasruddin stories are told aloud across Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim cultures, often as a joke followed by a quiet moment of recognition; some Sufi teachers use them as teaching tales.

games.q: you're on your knees in the street helping Nasruddin find his key. after an hour, you ask where he dropped it. what does he say?
o: inside the house, but there's more light out here.
games.why: inside the house. but there's more light out here. first you laugh at the fool; then you notice he's you.

practice: Think of something bigger than a key that you've been searching for lately: calm, confidence, a better night's sleep, a closer friendship. Ask honestly which lamp you've been looking under, and where you actually lost it.
Don't solve it; just let the answer point toward the house.

wordCard.voice: Nasruddin. A folk trickster who searches the street for a key he lost inside, because the light is better out there.

orig.note: Persian, Mulla Nasruddin: mulla is a title for a learned man. In Turkish he is Nasreddin Hoca (Hodja), from Persian khwaja, master.

carryVoice: Your line: search where you lost it. A good lamp can't find what isn't there. See you tomorrow.
